newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks to suffer as corporate ties loosen.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks to suffer as corporate ties loosen.

text.p: Fierce competition and radical restructuring plans are spurring many Japanese firms to shed share holdings in their business partners, and share prices are set to suffer as a result, analysts say.

The decline of the time-honoured Japanese practice of cross-shareholding is likely to weigh particularly heavily on the banking sector, which was already hit by sell-offs early this year on concerns over Japanese banks' financial health.

"Corporate shareholders -- insurers, banks, brokerages and other similar companies are trying to speed up the dissolution of mututal shareholdings," said Hitoshi Morimura, chief portfolio manager at Meiji Life Insurance Co's equity department.
"The potential for the unwinding of cross-shareholdings in the financial sector is high, but it could also happen to shares in any companies involved in cross-shareholdings," he said.
"Unrealised losses on shares are growing, so companies have begun asking themselves why they should run the risk of continuing to hold them," he added.
Japanese companies customarily hold part of their business partners' shares to cement ties and to protect themselves from mergers and acquisitions.

But the dissolution of cross-shareholdings has steadily accelerated since 1990, after the frenzy of share purchases during the asset bubble of the late 1980s left corporations holding too many stocks, said Makoto Takano, senior analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research Ltd.
In March 1996, cross-shareholdings at Japan's listed companies totalled about 37.8 percent of aggregate stock market value, down modestly from a peak of 43.1 percent 17 years ago, Takano said.

Some banks, brokerages and construction companies facing losses from problem loans or debt burdens have also been selling of each others' shares in an effort to cover part of those losses, brokers said.

Companies also sold bank shares when prices in the sector tumbled early this year, but most showed restraint, fearing that aggressive selling would fuel a melt-down in the shares and inflate their losses on share holdings as they prepared to close the books on fiscal 1996/97, which ended March 31.
With the start of the new fiscal year on April 1, however, companies would be more willing to sell shares, brokers said.

Takano said that Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms, expected to cause a shake-out in the financial industry, are also likely to accelerate the unloading of bank shares by Japanese firms, since they would be able to raise more funds in the capital markets and would be less dependent on bank loans.
"As restructuring accelerates, companies would prefer not to hold underperforming shares," he added.
Japanese insurers and corporations hold a high percentage of bank shares relative to other investors, noted Kazuhiro Miyake, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center.
Bank shares account for 35.6 percent of the overall shareholdings of Japanese corporations and 23.7 percent of insurers' holdings, compared with 10 to 15 percent for other investors.
"They will likely continue to unwind cross-shareholdings with banks, which could put heavy pressure on bank shares for a long time," he said.
